definition: Desiccated means completely dried out, with all the moisture removed.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word desiccated. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know desiccated should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The lunchbox came back from camp with one desiccated orange rattling around inside it like a maraca.
Dry is a state any towel reaches by evening — nothing to write home about, and nothing like desiccated, which means every drop drawn out of a thing all the way through.
Parched goes further than dry — cracked, gasping, drought-deep; desiccated claims the most: the water is gone from inside the thing, and no single rain puts it back.

Dried-out is the plain, everyday phrase for a thing that has lost its moisture — bread, markers, garden beds. Desiccated adds completely and clinically: every drop removed, all the way through, the way a lab or a desert does it.

Shriveled describes the shape drying leaves behind — skin puckered, edges curled, a thing shrunk into wrinkles. Desiccated reports the water itself gone from inside, whatever the surface looks like. A raisin is shriveled; museum wood is desiccated.

Latin siccus, "dry," survives in English almost nowhere — except the little packet marked desiccant that ships inside shoeboxes and camera bags, there to drink up moisture before it reaches the goods. Same family, same job; beyond that, the root's line ends here.
Desiccated means completely dried out, with all the moisture removed.

Every guitar that moves to the high desert fights the same war, and the Santa Fe repair shop keeps a shelf of the losers: tops split along the grain, bridges lifted, one mandolin whose back opened like a seed pod.
Wood cut in humid lowlands carries water in every cell, and a winter of furnace air leaves it desiccated — not dry to the touch but dry all the way through, shrunken past the builder's numbers.
The waiting room runs a humidifier the size of a stove.
Desiccated is the exact word for that wood, because it means dried up, with the moisture removed — removed being the working part.
Dry names a state; desiccated reports a process finished, the water taken out of a thing's very tissue, which is why it suits old wood, forgotten fruit, and lab samples better than a sunny afternoon.
Desiccated is the laboratory's and the archaeologist's word — reach for it when the drying is total and the point of the sentence.
A dry summer, a parched lawn, a shriveled apple each keep their everyday word.
Beside this unit's desolate, note what is missing in each: a desiccated thing has lost its water; a desolate place has lost its people.

The seed bank's basement holds a quiet paradox: the driest room in the county exists to keep things alive.
Every sample that arrives — beans, prairie grasses, apple pips — is desiccated before storage: two weeks in a chamber of cold, moving air until almost no water remains in the seed at all.
The point is not tidiness.
Water is what lets time act on a seed; take out every last trace of it, and the clock inside nearly stops.
A curator showed visitors two jars: pips stored on a pantry shelf, soft and mottled after five years, and pips from the chamber, hard as gravel after forty.
'A kitchen gets things sort of dry,' she said, tapping the second jar.
'We are after something absolute — moisture gone from the inside out.'
